title: Graph theory and extremal combinatorics
blurb: Trees, bipartite graphs, the theorems of Mantel, Turán and Hall, and small Ramsey numbers, with the extremal arguments that prove them and the olympiad problems they solve.
outcomes: Translate a problem into a graph and use degrees, trees and odd cycles to prove structural facts
Prove and apply Mantel, Turán and Hall, and find the matching extremal constructions
Run longest-path, shortest-odd-cycle and maximum-degree arguments to olympiad standard
lesson:
Among ten people there are $26$ pairs of friends. Prove that some three of them are mutual friends.

Suppose not. Write $d(v)$ for the number of friends of $v$. If $x$ and $y$ are friends, they have no common friend, so $d(x)+d(y)\le 10$. Add this over all $26$ friendships. Each person $v$ appears in $d(v)$ of these inequalities, so the left-hand side adds up to $\sum_v d(v)^2$, and by the QM-AM inequality \[ \sum_v d(v)^2\ \ge\ \frac{1}{10}\Big(\sum_v d(v)\Big)^2=\frac{52^2}{10} > 260=26\cdot 10. \] This contradicts the bound, so three mutual friends exist. The same computation shows that a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices has at most $n^2/4$ edges (Mantel's theorem), and $26 > 100/4$.

This unit collects the graph theory that BMO2, EGMO and USAMO combinatorics assume: trees, bipartite graphs, the theorems of Mantel, Turán and Hall, and small Ramsey numbers. I assume the extremal principle from L4-CO1 and double counting from L4-CO2; most proofs below are one of those two ideas applied to the right object.

Language

A graph $G$ is a finite set $V$ of vertices with a set $E$ of edges, each edge an unordered pair of distinct vertices; $n=|V|$ and $e=|E|$. The degree $d(v)$ is the number of edges at $v$, and $N(v)$ is the set of neighbours of $v$. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive ones adjacent; a cycle is a path of at least three vertices whose ends are also adjacent, and its length is its number of edges. $G$ is connected if any two vertices are joined by a path; the maximal connected pieces are the components. A set of vertices is independent if it contains no edge, and a clique if it contains every possible edge. $K_n$ is the complete graph, and $K_{a,b}$ the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes $a$ and $b$.

Theorem 1 (Handshake lemma). $\sum_{v\in V}d(v)=2e$. In particular, the number of vertices of odd degree is even.

Proof. Each edge is counted once from each of its two ends. $\blacksquare$

Trees

A tree is a connected graph with no cycle; a forest is a graph with no cycle, so its components are trees. A leaf is a vertex of degree $1$.

Theorem 2. (a) Every tree with $n\ge2$ vertices has at least two leaves. (b) A tree with $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges, and a forest with $n$ vertices and $c$ components has $n-c$ edges. (c) A connected graph with $n$ vertices and $n-1$ edges is a tree.

Proof. (a) Take a longest path $x_0x_1\dots x_k$ (extremal principle); $k\ge1$ since there is an edge. Every neighbour of $x_0$ lies on the path, or the path could be extended. If $x_0$ were adjacent to some $x_i$ with $i\ge2$, then $x_0x_1\dots x_ix_0$ would be a cycle. So $d(x_0)=1$, and similarly $d(x_k)=1$.

(b) Induct on $n$. Deleting a leaf from a tree with $n\ge2$ vertices leaves a tree with one vertex and one edge fewer. For a forest, add the formula over the components.

(c) While the graph has a cycle, delete one edge of a cycle; this keeps it connected, since the rest of the cycle still joins the two ends. We finish with a tree, which by (b) has $n-1$ edges, so no edge was deleted. $\blacksquare$

Note that the longest-path argument proves more: if every vertex has degree at least $d\ge 2$, then the end $x_0$ has at least $d$ neighbours on the path, the furthest being some $x_i$ with $i\ge d$, so $G$ has a cycle of length at least $d+1$. Longest paths will come back in the practice problems.

Example 1. In how many ways can the integers $1,2,\dots,100$ be coloured red and blue so that no two different integers of the same colour add up to a power of $2$?

Make a graph on $\{1,\dots,100\}$, joining $a$ and $b$ when $a+b$ is a power of $2$. A valid colouring is a colouring with no edge inside a colour class, so we want to know whether this graph is bipartite and how many components it has. Draw it for $1,\dots,15$ first.

The picture is a forest, and the reason is visible: each number has at most one smaller neighbour. Indeed, if $a < b$ and $a+b=2^k$, then $b < 2^k < 2b$, and the open interval $(b,2b)$ contains at most one power of $2$, because consecutive powers of $2$ differ by a factor of $2$. It contains none if $b$ is a power of $2$, and exactly one otherwise.

A graph in which every vertex has at most one smaller neighbour has no cycle: the largest vertex of a cycle would have two smaller neighbours on it. So the graph is a forest. The numbers up to $100$ with no smaller neighbour are $1,2,4,8,16,32,64$, so the number of edges is $100-7=93$, and by Theorem 2(b) there are $100-93=7$ components.

A tree has exactly two proper $2$-colourings: colour any vertex, and the colour of every other vertex is forced along the unique path to it, with no conflict since there is no cycle. Colourings of different components are independent, so the answer is $2^7=128$.

Bipartite graphs and odd cycles

$G$ is bipartite if $V$ splits into two independent sets, that is, if $G$ has a proper colouring with two colours.

Theorem 3. A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no cycle of odd length.

Proof. A cycle in a bipartite graph alternates between the parts, so it has even length. Conversely, suppose there is no odd cycle. First, a closed walk of odd length contains an odd cycle: if no vertex repeats it is a cycle; if some vertex repeats, the walk splits at it into two shorter closed walks whose lengths add to an odd number, so one of them is odd, and we induct on the length. Now work in one component, fix a vertex $r$, and colour each vertex by the parity of its distance from $r$. If two adjacent vertices $u$, $v$ had the same colour, then a shortest path from $r$ to $u$, the edge $uv$ and a shortest path from $v$ back to $r$ would form a closed walk of odd length $\operatorname{dist}(r,u)+\operatorname{dist}(r,v)+1$, hence an odd cycle. $\blacksquare$

In practice, use Theorem 3 in both directions: to show a colouring exists, rule out odd cycles; to show a graph is not bipartite, exhibit one. In extremal problems a shortest odd cycle is often the right object, since it has no chords (a chord would split it into two shorter cycles, one of them odd).

Mantel and Turán

Theorem 4 (Mantel). A triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices has at most $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ edges, with equality only for $K_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\lceil n/2\rceil}$.

Proof. Let $v$ have the largest degree $\Delta$. Since $G$ has no triangle, $N(v)$ is independent, so every edge has an end in $S=V\setminus N(v)$, a set of $n-\Delta$ vertices each of degree at most $\Delta$. Hence \[ e\ \le\ \sum_{s\in S}d(s)\ \le\ (n-\Delta)\Delta\ \le\ \frac{n^2}{4}. \] For equality every inequality must be tight: no edge has both ends in $S$, every $s\in S$ has degree $\Delta=|N(v)|$ and so is adjacent to all of $N(v)$, and $\Delta(n-\Delta)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ forces $\{\Delta,n-\Delta\}=\{\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\lceil n/2\rceil\}$. So $G$ is complete bipartite with parts $S$ and $N(v)$. $\blacksquare$

Theorem 5 (Turán). If a graph on $n$ vertices contains no $K_{r+1}$, then $e\le\left(1-\frac1r\right)\frac{n^2}{2}$.

Proof. Induct on $r$; for $r=1$ there are no edges. Let $r\ge2$ and let $v$ have the largest degree $\Delta$. The graph induced on $N(v)$ has no $K_r$ (with $v$ it would give a $K_{r+1}$), so by induction it has at most $\big(1-\frac{1}{r-1}\big)\frac{\Delta^2}{2}$ edges. Every other edge has an end in $V\setminus N(v)$, so there are at most $(n-\Delta)\Delta$ of them. Therefore \[ e\ \le\ \frac{r-2}{r-1}\cdot\frac{\Delta^2}{2}+(n-\Delta)\Delta\ =\ n\Delta-\frac{r}{2(r-1)}\Delta^2\ \le\ \frac{r-1}{r}\cdot\frac{n^2}{2}, \] where the last step is the maximum of a quadratic in $\Delta$, attained at $\Delta=\frac{r-1}{r}n$. $\blacksquare$

The bound is attained when $r\mid n$ by the complete $r$-partite graph with equal parts. (For general $n$ the exact maximum is the number of edges of the complete $r$-partite graph with parts as equal as possible; the proof is the same with more care, and you will rarely need it.)

Example 2. Twelve distinct points lie in a closed disc of radius $1$. At most how many of the $66$ pairs of points can be at distance greater than $\sqrt2$?

Join two points when their distance exceeds $\sqrt2$. Since $\sqrt2$ is the side of a square inscribed in the circle, test four points: can four points be pairwise more than $\sqrt2$ apart? If one of them is the centre $O$, it is within $1$ of the others. Otherwise the four rays from $O$ through the points divide the full angle, so two of them make an angle $\theta\le90^\circ$. For those two points $P$, $Q$, the cosine rule gives \[ PQ^2=OP^2+OQ^2-2\,OP\cdot OQ\cos\theta\ \le\ OP^2+OQ^2\ \le\ 2. \] So the graph has no $K_4$, and Theorem 5 with $r=3$ gives at most $\frac23\cdot\frac{144}{2}=48$ edges.

The equality case of Turán's theorem tells us what to build: three groups of four with every pair from different groups far apart. Put four points very close to each vertex of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle. Points in different groups are at distance close to $\sqrt3 > \sqrt2$, so $3\cdot4\cdot4=48$ pairs are far apart. The answer is $48$.

Hall's theorem

A matching is a set of edges with no common ends. In a bipartite graph with parts $A$ and $B$, for $S\subseteq A$ write $N(S)$ for the set of vertices of $B$ adjacent to some vertex of $S$.

Theorem 6 (Hall). A bipartite graph with parts $A$, $B$ has a matching covering every vertex of $A$ if and only if $|N(S)|\ge|S|$ for every $S\subseteq A$.

Proof. The condition is necessary, since the partners of $S$ are $|S|$ distinct vertices of $N(S)$. For sufficiency, induct on $|A|$; the case $|A|=1$ is clear. There are two cases.

Case 1: $|N(S)|\ge|S|+1$ for every non-empty $S\subsetneq A$. Match any $a\in A$ with any neighbour $b$ and delete both. In the remaining graph each non-empty $S\subseteq A\setminus\{a\}$ has lost at most the one neighbour $b$, so it still has at least $|S|$ neighbours, and induction finishes.

Case 2: some non-empty $S_0\subsetneq A$ has $|N(S_0)|=|S_0|$. Hall's condition holds inside the graph on $S_0\cup N(S_0)$, so by induction $S_0$ can be matched into $N(S_0)$. In the graph on $(A\setminus S_0)\cup(B\setminus N(S_0))$, a set $T\subseteq A\setminus S_0$ has neighbourhood $N(T\cup S_0)\setminus N(S_0)$, of size at least $|T|+|S_0|-|S_0|=|T|$. So induction matches $A\setminus S_0$ there too, and the two matchings together cover $A$. $\blacksquare$

Corollary 7. If every vertex of a bipartite graph (multiple edges allowed) has degree $k\ge1$, it has a perfect matching.

Proof. The $k|S|$ edges leaving $S\subseteq A$ all end in $N(S)$, which receives $k|N(S)|$ edges in total, so $|N(S)|\ge|S|$. Also $k|A|=e=k|B|$, so a matching covering $A$ is perfect. $\blacksquare$

Example 3. Each of the numbers $1,2,\dots,6$ is written in six cells of a $6\times6$ table, one number per cell. Prove that one can choose a cell in each column so that the six chosen numbers are all different.

Trying to choose column by column fails: an early greedy choice can use up the only number that some later column could take. This is a matching problem, so set it up as one. Let $A$ be the six columns and $B$ the six numbers, and join column $c$ to number $k$ if $k$ appears in $c$. We need a matching covering $A$.

Check Hall's condition. A set $S$ of columns contains $6|S|$ cells, and every number in them belongs to $N(S)$. Each number occupies only six cells of the whole table, so the cells of $S$ hold at most $6|N(S)|$ entries. Hence $6|S|\le6|N(S)|$, and Theorem 6 gives the matching. (Equivalently: join column $c$ to number $k$ by one edge for each appearance of $k$ in $c$; this multigraph is $6$-regular, and Corollary 7 applies.)

Ramsey numbers

$R(s,t)$ is the least $n$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_n$ has a red $K_s$ or a blue $K_t$.

Theorem 8. $R(3,3)=6$, and $R(s,t)\le R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)$ for $s,t\ge2$.

Proof. Let $n=R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)$ and fix a vertex $v$ of a coloured $K_n$. Its $n-1$ edges split into $r$ red and $b$ blue with $r+b=n-1$, so $r\ge R(s-1,t)$ or $b\ge R(s,t-1)$. In the first case the red neighbours of $v$ contain a blue $K_t$, or a red $K_{s-1}$ which with $v$ is a red $K_s$; the second case is symmetric. With $R(2,3)=R(3,2)=3$ this gives $R(3,3)\le6$, and the pentagon with red sides and blue diagonals shows $R(3,3) > 5$. $\blacksquare$

The values worth remembering are $R(3,3)=6$, $R(3,4)=9$, $R(3,5)=14$ and $R(4,4)=18$. Theorem 8 gives only $R(3,4)\le10$; the improvement to $9$ is a parity argument (practice problem 2). That $R(4,4) > 17$ needs a specific colouring of $K_{17}$ (Greenwood and Gleason, 1955), which I will not reproduce. Lower bounds for large $k$ come from the counting argument in L5-CO2.

Extremal arguments on graphs

Each proof above began by choosing an extreme object: a longest path, a vertex of largest degree, a set $S_0$ on which Hall's condition is tight. The last example adds one more choice: a subgraph obtained by deleting vertices of small degree.

Example 4. A graph has $30$ vertices and $121$ edges. Prove that it contains a copy of every tree with $5$ edges.

The numbers are $121 > 4\cdot30$, which suggests the general statement: a graph with $n$ vertices and more than $(k-1)n$ edges contains every tree with $k$ edges. Large average degree alone does not obviously help, because the edges might be concentrated on a few vertices. Large minimum degree does, so we first find a subgraph where every degree is large.

Step 1. Repeatedly delete a vertex whose degree in the current graph is at most $k-1$. If this deleted every vertex, it would remove all edges, at most $k-1$ with each deletion, so $e\le(k-1)n$, a contradiction. So the process stops at a non-empty subgraph $H$ in which every degree is at least $k$.

Step 2. Let $T$ be a tree with $k$ edges, hence $k+1$ vertices. Order its vertices $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_k$ so that each $t_i$ with $i\ge1$ has exactly one neighbour among $t_0,\dots,t_{i-1}$ (repeatedly remove a leaf, and reverse the order of removal). Place $t_0$ at any vertex of $H$. When $t_0,\dots,t_{i-1}$ have been placed at distinct vertices, $t_i$ must go to a neighbour of the image of its earlier neighbour $t_j$. That image has at least $k$ neighbours in $H$, and at most $i-1\le k-1$ of them are already used (all placed vertices except the image of $t_j$ itself). So a free neighbour exists, and the embedding never gets stuck.

With $n=30$ and $k=5$ this proves the claim. The constant $k-1$ is not best possible; a conjecture of Erdős and Sós asserts that more than $\frac{k-1}{2}n$ edges suffice, and that is open in general.

Common traps.

  • Assuming a graph is connected. Theorem 2(b) has $n-c$, not $n-1$, for forests; problems about "a network" often need connectivity stated or proved.
  • Proving the bound in an extremal problem and forgetting the construction, or the reverse. "Find the maximum" needs both.
  • Applying Hall to the wrong side. The condition is checked for subsets of the side you want covered.
  • In a longest path argument, forgetting to say why every neighbour of the end lies on the path.
  • Quoting Turán with the wrong $r$: no $K_{r+1}$ gives $(1-\frac1r)\frac{n^2}{2}$.

How to spot this in a contest

Whenever a problem has people and friendships, cities and roads, or objects and a symmetric relation, draw the graph and translate. Then the standard moves, roughly in the order I try them, are:

  1. count degrees (handshake lemma, double counting edges or paths of length $2$);
  2. take an extreme object: a longest path, a shortest odd cycle, a vertex of largest or smallest degree;
  3. if the question is about two-colouring or splitting into two groups, look for odd cycles (Theorem 3);
  4. if a forbidden subgraph is a triangle or a clique, compare with Mantel or Turán, and expect the extremal example to be complete multipartite;
  5. if each object must be assigned its own distinct partner, set up a bipartite graph and check Hall's condition;
  6. if a statement is "every colouring contains a monochromatic ...", fix a vertex and use pigeonhole on its edges, as in Theorem 8.

practice.q: A tree has a vertex of degree $10$ and a vertex of degree $7$. What is the smallest possible number of leaves?
practice.hint: Use the handshake lemma and $e=n-1$ to express the number of leaves in terms of the degrees greater than $2$.
practice.sol:
Let the tree have $n$ vertices, $n_1$ of them leaves. By Theorem 2 it has $n-1$ edges, so the handshake lemma gives $\sum_v d(v)=2n-2$, that is, $\sum_v\big(d(v)-2\big)=-2$. Leaves contribute $-1$ each, vertices of degree $2$ contribute $0$, and no vertex has degree $0$ (a tree with a vertex of degree $10$ has $n\ge2$ and is connected). Hence \[ n_1=2+\sum_{d(v)\ge3}\big(d(v)-2\big)\ \ge\ 2+(10-2)+(7-2)=15. \]

Equality is possible: take adjacent vertices $u$ and $w$, attach $9$ leaves to $u$ and $6$ leaves to $w$. This is a tree with $17$ vertices, $d(u)=10$, $d(w)=7$ and $15$ leaves. The answer is $15$.

practice.q: Prove that among any nine people there are three mutual friends or four mutual strangers.
practice.hint: Assume not. How many friends can one person have? How many strangers? Then use the handshake lemma.
practice.sol:
Suppose nine people have neither three mutual friends nor four mutual strangers, and consider the friendship graph. Fix a person $v$.

The friends of $v$ are pairwise strangers, since two friends of $v$ who were friends would form three mutual friends with $v$. There are no four mutual strangers, so $v$ has at most $3$ friends.

Among the strangers of $v$ there are no three mutual strangers (with $v$ they would make four) and no three mutual friends. Since $R(3,3)=6$, $v$ has at most $5$ strangers. So $v$ has at least $8-5=3$ friends.

Hence every one of the nine people has exactly $3$ friends, and the sum of the degrees is $27$, which is odd. This contradicts the handshake lemma. So three mutual friends or four mutual strangers exist.

(This shows $R(3,4)\le9$. Equality holds: put eight people around a circle and make two of them friends when they are $1$ or $4$ places apart. One can check that there are no three mutual friends and no four mutual strangers.)

practice.q: In a graph every vertex has degree at least $3$. Prove that it has a cycle whose length is not divisible by $3$.
practice.hint: Take a longest path. Its first vertex has at least three neighbours, all on the path, so you get three cycles.
practice.sol:
Let $x_0x_1\dots x_k$ be a longest path in the graph. Every neighbour of $x_0$ lies on the path, since otherwise the path could be extended at $x_0$. As $d(x_0)\ge3$, the vertex $x_0$ has neighbours $x_1$, $x_i$ and $x_j$ with $1 < i < j\le k$.

Consider the three cycles \[ x_0x_1\dots x_ix_0,\qquad x_0x_1\dots x_jx_0,\qquad x_0x_ix_{i+1}\dots x_jx_0, \] which are genuine cycles because the vertices of the path are distinct and $i\ge2$. Their lengths are $i+1$, $j+1$ and $j-i+2$. If the first two are divisible by $3$, then $i\equiv j\equiv2\pmod 3$, so $j-i+2\equiv2\pmod3$, and the third cycle has length not divisible by $3$. Otherwise one of the first two already works.

practice.q: In a $7\times7$ table, exactly $3$ cells in each row and exactly $3$ cells in each column are marked. Prove that the marked cells can be coloured red, green and blue so that each row and each column contains one marked cell of each colour.
practice.hint: Rows and columns are the two parts of a bipartite graph whose edges are the marked cells. What does Corollary 7 give, and what is left after removing it?
practice.sol:
Form a bipartite graph whose parts are the $7$ rows and the $7$ columns, with one edge between row $r$ and column $c$ for each marked cell $(r,c)$. Every vertex has degree $3$. A colouring as required is the same as a partition of the edges into three perfect matchings, the red, green and blue cells.

We prove by induction on $k$ that a bipartite graph in which every vertex has degree $k\ge1$ splits into $k$ perfect matchings. By Corollary 7 (which follows from Hall's theorem) it has a perfect matching $M$. Removing the edges of $M$ lowers every degree by exactly $1$, because $M$ covers every vertex exactly once. If $k=1$ the graph is $M$ itself; otherwise the rest is $(k-1)$-regular and splits into $k-1$ perfect matchings by induction.

Applying this with $k=3$ and colouring the cells of the three matchings red, green and blue, each row and each column meets each matching in exactly one edge, so it contains one marked cell of each colour.

practice.q: Among nine people there are exactly $27$ pairs of friends. Prove that there are at least $27$ sets of three mutual friends, and show that $27$ can occur.
practice.hint: Two friends $x$ and $y$ have at least $d(x)+d(y)-9$ common friends. Add this over all friendships and count what you get.
practice.sol:
Write $d(v)$ for the number of friends of $v$, and $T$ for the number of sets of three mutual friends. Let $x$ and $y$ be friends. Among the other $7$ people, $x$ has $d(x)-1$ friends and $y$ has $d(y)-1$ friends, so they have at least $(d(x)-1)+(d(y)-1)-7=d(x)+d(y)-9$ common friends.

Each set of three mutual friends contains three friendships, and is counted once for each of them when we add up the numbers of common friends over all friendships. Hence \[ 3T\ \ge\ \sum_{xy\text{ friends}}\big(d(x)+d(y)-9\big)=\sum_v d(v)^2-9\cdot27, \] since $v$ appears in exactly $d(v)$ friendships. By the handshake lemma $\sum_v d(v)=54$, so by the QM-AM inequality $\sum_v d(v)^2\ge\frac{54^2}{9}=324$. Therefore $3T\ge324-243=81$ and $T\ge27$.

For equality, split the people into three groups of three and make two people friends exactly when they are in different groups. There are $3\cdot3\cdot3=27$ friendships, and a set of three is a set of mutual friends exactly when it has one person from each group, so there are $27$ such sets.

(The same argument shows that any graph with $n$ vertices and $e$ edges has at least $\frac{e(4e-n^2)}{3n}$ triangles, which is positive as soon as $e > n^2/4$; this is a quantitative form of Mantel's theorem.)

practice.q: In a club of $n$ members no three are mutual friends, and every member has more than $\frac{2n}{5}$ friends. Prove that the members can be split into two groups so that no two members of the same group are friends.
practice.hint: By Theorem 3 it suffices to rule out odd cycles. Take a shortest odd cycle and ask how many neighbours a vertex can have on it.
practice.sol:
Consider the friendship graph $G$. By Theorem 3 it suffices to show that $G$ has no odd cycle. Suppose it has one, and let $C$ be an odd cycle of smallest length $m$. Since there is no triangle, $m\ge5$.

Claim 1: two vertices of $C$ are adjacent only if they are consecutive on $C$. A chord would split $C$ into two cycles of lengths $a+1$ and $b+1$, where $a,b\ge2$ and $a+b=m$. One of $a+1$, $b+1$ is odd, because their sum $m+2$ is odd, and both are less than $m$. This contradicts the minimality of $m$. So every vertex of $C$ has exactly $2$ neighbours on $C$.

Claim 2: a vertex $v$ not on $C$ has at most $2$ neighbours on $C$. Suppose $v$ has three neighbours on $C$. They cut $C$ into three arcs of lengths $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\ge1$ with $\ell_1+\ell_2+\ell_3=m$, and each arc together with $v$ forms a cycle of length $\ell_i+2$. Since $m$ is odd, either exactly one $\ell_i$ is odd or all three are. If exactly one, say $\ell_1$, is odd, then $\ell_2,\ell_3\ge2$, so $\ell_1\le m-4$ and the cycle of length $\ell_1+2\le m-2$ is odd and shorter than $C$. If all three are odd, take the smallest, $\ell_1\le\frac m3$; then $\ell_1+2\le\frac m3+2 < m$ because $m\ge5$, and again we have a shorter odd cycle. Both cases contradict the minimality of $m$.

Now count the edges between $C$ and $V$ in two ways. Every vertex of $G$, on $C$ or not, has at most $2$ neighbours on $C$, so \[ \sum_{c\in C}d(c)=\sum_{v\in V}|N(v)\cap C|\ \le\ 2n. \] But each of the $m\ge5$ vertices of $C$ has degree greater than $\frac{2n}{5}$, so the left-hand side exceeds $5\cdot\frac{2n}{5}=2n$. This contradiction shows that $G$ has no odd cycle, so $G$ is bipartite, which is the required split.

(This is a theorem of Andrásfai, Erdős and Sós. The constant is best possible: replace each vertex of a $5$-cycle by a group of $k$ members, with members of adjacent groups friends. Then $n=5k$, each member has exactly $2k=\frac{2n}{5}$ friends, there is no triangle, and the $5$-cycle through one member of each group is odd.)

ladder.note: Fix one person and apply pigeonhole to the three topics; then you are left with a two-colour question.
If two children are at distance k in the friendship graph, how far apart can they stand in the line?
Count pairs of balls sharing a box in two ways, then construct an example meeting the bound.
For each question, look at the set of children who got it wrong, and see what the condition says about two such sets.
Rows and columns form a bipartite graph for each colour; check Hall's condition.
For the lower bound, find a large family of diagonals that pairwise cross; then look for a colouring that matches it.
Look for six points all of whose fifteen edges are coloured.
Consider how many sets the most popular element lies in, and split into cases.
Make a graph on the cells, take a spanning tree, and look for an edge whose removal leaves two large pieces.
Find properties of the graph that the moves can be made to preserve, and reduce the number of vertices one at a time.
